name: Skier's / gamekeeper's thumb (thumb UCL injury)
summary: A valgus-abduction force at the thumb MCP joint tears the ulnar collateral ligament, usually at its distal attachment. A Stener lesion will not heal in a cast and usually needs surgery.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Partial tears: nonoperative care usually favoured. Complete tears: surgery recommended; athletes returned to sport within 5–8 weeks of surgery in a review (up to 98.1%)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Valgus stress at 0° and 30° of MCP flexion: no firm endpoint suggests a complete tear

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Ultrasound for a Stener lesion: pooled sensitivity 96% and specificity 90% (17 studies); MRI 93% and 98% in a separate meta-analysis

keyFacts.label: Stener lesion
keyFacts.value: 51.4% of 35 surgically treated soldiers had one; 95% of 262 hand surgeons favour surgery for it

keyFacts.label: Skiing context
keyFacts.value: Isolated UCL lesions were 16.9% of 195 distal upper limb ski injuries in one two-season study

keyFacts.label: Evidence quality
keyFacts.value: No randomised trials of operative versus nonoperative care were found; evidence is cohorts, reviews and surveys

overview:
The ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) of the thumb metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint resists valgus (radial-directed) stress, and its injury causes pain and instability, especially in key pinch and grasp [r1]. Collateral ligament injuries of the thumb MCP joint occur through forced abduction or hyperextension [r2]. The terms are often mixed: 'skier's thumb' is an acute injury from a fall onto an abducted thumb or a valgus force, while 'gamekeeper's thumb' strictly means a chronic injury in which the ligament becomes attenuated through repetitive stress [r3]. The UCL most commonly ruptures at its distal insertion [r4].

When a complete rupture occurs, the adductor aponeurosis can become interposed between the retracted UCL stump and its insertion on the proximal phalanx. This is a Stener lesion [r1], first described by Bertil Stener in 1962 [r4]. A complete rupture at the distal insertion commonly cannot heal without surgery because of the interposed aponeurosis, while a partial or non-displaced tear can usually be managed nonoperatively [r4]. A valgus stress test with a firm endpoint indicates a partial tear and favours nonoperative treatment, while no firm endpoint indicates a complete tear, for which operative treatment is recommended [r3]. Ultrasound is accurate for Stener lesions [r5,r6], but comparative trials of operative and nonoperative care are lacking [r7,r8].

epidemiology.text:
Upper extremity injuries account for 20–35% of all alpine skiing injuries, and sprain of the thumb MCP joint UCL is the most common upper extremity injury in skiing [r9]. In a two-season study of 195 adults with distal upper limb ski and snowboard injuries in the Italian Dolomites, 33 (16.9%) had isolated UCL lesions. These occurred mainly on red slopes (54.5%) and were often related to pole entrapment during falls. None of the injured patients reported using protective wrist or thumb supports [r10]. A systematic review reported that UCL injuries account for approximately 86% of injuries affecting the base of the thumb [r8].

The injury is not confined to skiing. A review describes it as common in athletes generally [r2], and a retrospective series of 35 operated active-duty soldiers found that rifle-related injuries (60.0%) were the most common mechanism [r11]. Population incidence figures were not retrieved from the sources used for this page, so none are quoted.

intrinsic: Chronic UCL attenuation from repetitive radial stress (the 'gamekeeper's' pattern), which makes acute rupture easier [r3]
Previous thumb MCP sprain or generalised ligament laxity (clinical reasoning)
Reduced hand protection reflexes in fatigue late in the day (clinical reasoning)
extrinsic: Falling with a ski pole in the hand: pole entrapment during falls was often reported [r10]
Forced thumb abduction from a ball, equipment or an opponent in contact sports [r2]
Rifle handling and other military activities that generate valgus stress [r11]
No protective thumb support, which none of the injured skiers had used [r10]

mechanism.summary: The classic injury is a fall onto an outstretched hand with the thumb abducted, often with the ski pole handle gripped, so that the handle or the ground levers the thumb into valgus (abduction) at the MCP joint [r10,r3]. The UCL is loaded beyond its capacity and fails, usually at its distal attachment on the proximal phalanx [r4]. Forced abduction or hyperextension are the recognised mechanisms [r2].
sequence: The skier falls with the ski pole strap around the wrist and the handle gripped, with the thumb abducted along the handle [r10].
The hand strikes the snow, and the handle or the ground drives the thumb into abduction at the MCP joint [r2].
The UCL, which resists valgus stress, is loaded first in tension (clinical reasoning).
The ligament fails, most commonly at its distal insertion on the base of the proximal phalanx, and it may avulse a bone fragment [r4,r12].
In a partial tear the remaining fibres hold the joint with a firm endpoint on valgus stress [r3].

In a complete tear the proximal ligament end retracts. The adductor aponeurosis can slide between the stump and its insertion (a Stener lesion) [r1], and on ultrasound displaced tears most commonly lie proximal to the aponeurosis [r13].
The thumb MCP joint becomes unstable in pinch, and persistent instability can reduce grip strength and lead to early MCP osteoarthritis [r4].

variants.name: Acute 'skier's' injury
variants.description: A fall onto an abducted thumb or a valgus force on the abducted thumb in athletes [r3].

variants.name: Chronic 'gamekeeper's' injury
variants.description: Repetitive radial stress attenuates the ligament over time [r3]. Chronic injuries are effectively treated with ligament reconstruction [r2,r7].

variants.name: Stener lesion
variants.description: Complete rupture with the adductor aponeurosis interposed between the retracted stump and its insertion [r1].

variants.name: Avulsion fracture
variants.description: A bone fragment pulls off with the ligament. In 114 patients the fragment size approximated the UCL footprint, and MCP instability rather than fragment size was associated with surgery [r12].

variants.name: Proximal rupture and pseudo-Stener lesion
variants.description: A rare proximal rupture can present with a mass that mimics a Stener lesion but is granulation tissue, as in one case report [r4].

variants.name: Combined collateral and extensor injury
variants.description: In a selected ultrasound cohort of 42 patients, UCL pathology was present in 83.3%, radial collateral ligament pathology in 54.8%, and dorsal extensor-related abnormalities in 40.5% [r14].

anatomy.text: The thumb MCP joint is stabilised by the proper and accessory collateral ligaments, the volar and dorsal plates and the adductor pollicis aponeurosis [r15]. The UCL runs from the metacarpal head to the ulnar base of the proximal phalanx. On MRI in healthy volunteers it is typically striated and less than 3 mm thick, whereas the radial collateral ligament is less than 2 mm thick. A full-thickness synovial recess at the base of the dorsal plate is a normal finding and should not be mistaken for a tear [r15]. The adductor aponeurosis lies superficial to the UCL, and its proximal edge is the landmark for the Stener lesion [r1,r13]. The proper UCL is taut in flexion and the accessory ligament in extension (clinical anatomy), which is why testing is done in both positions [r3].

structures.name: Ulnar collateral ligament (UCL)
structures.role: Resists valgus stress at the thumb MCP joint and supports key pinch and grasp [r1]

structures.name: Adductor pollicis aponeurosis
structures.role: Overlies the UCL. When the ligament ruptures distally, the aponeurosis can become interposed (Stener lesion) [r1]

structures.name: Radial collateral ligament (RCL)
structures.role: Resists varus stress and is injured in some cases along with the UCL [r14]

structures.name: Volar plate
structures.role: Limits MCP hyperextension. Hyperextension is one mechanism of collateral injury [r2]

structures.name: Extensor mechanism (EPB and EPL)
structures.role: Dorsal extensor-related abnormalities were found in 40.5% of a selected ultrasound cohort of thumb MCP collateral injuries [r14]

structures.name: Proximal phalanx base
structures.role: The distal attachment of the UCL, where avulsion fractures occur [r12]

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
The UCL fails when the valgus load exceeds its tensile capacity. Failure is most common at the distal insertion [r4], and can be partial (some fibres intact, firm endpoint) or complete (no endpoint) [r3]. Part of the insertion may avulse as a bone fragment [r12].

In a complete tear with a Stener lesion the adductor aponeurosis lies between the retracted ligament stump and its footprint, so the ends cannot meet and heal in a cast [r1,r4]. Even after surgery, there are no repair or reconstruction methods using native tissue that give strength equivalent to the pre-injured ligament, and suture tape augmentation has given excellent short-term results and earlier return to function, with little long-term data [r1]. Untreated instability can reduce grip strength and lead to early MCP osteoarthritis [r4].

structures.name: UCL
structures.effect: Partial or complete tear, mostly at the distal insertion; may avulse bone [r4,r12]

structures.name: Adductor aponeurosis
structures.effect: Interposed between the stump and the insertion in a Stener lesion [r1]

structures.name: Radial collateral ligament
structures.effect: Also abnormal on ultrasound in 54.8% of one selected cohort [r14]

structures.name: Dorsal extensor structures
structures.effect: Abnormal in 40.5% of that selected cohort, which suggests dorsal capsular or extensor damage in some injuries [r14]

structures.name: Proximal phalanx base
structures.effect: Avulsion fracture fragment; its size approximated the UCL footprint in 114 patients [r12]

muscles.name: Adductor pollicis
muscles.effect: Its aponeurosis forms the interposed layer in a Stener lesion, and the muscle's pull is needed for pinch [r1].

muscles.name: Thenar muscles and first dorsal interosseous
muscles.effect: Pain-related inhibition reduces key pinch strength, and immobilisation causes disuse weakness (clinical).

muscles.name: Forearm and wrist muscles
muscles.effect: Compensatory gripping through the other digits and wrist in the immobilised phase (clinical).

cellular.description: Torn vessels bleed, and platelets, neutrophils and macrophages clear debris at the rupture site (typical ligament-healing timeline; clinical).
Fibroblasts lay down disorganised type III collagen across the gap if the ends are apposed. A Stener lesion prevents the ends from meeting [r4].
Collagen aligns along the line of load and the scar matures. A repaired ligament does not regain the strength of the native ligament [r1].
Unrepaired or attenuated ligaments leave a lax joint and may need reconstruction [r7,r3].

systems.effect: Pain at the ulnar MCP joint inhibits pinch. Transient sensory disturbance was reported by 3 of 35 soldiers after repair, so the digital nerves are at risk in surgery [r11].
Local swelling and bruising on the ulnar side of the MCP joint follow the rupture (clinical).
Persistent instability reduces grip and may lead to MCP osteoarthritis [r4]; wrist and thumb CMC joint can be overloaded in compensation (clinical).
A thumb spica for weeks is disabling for skiers, athletes, soldiers and manual workers. Surgeons weigh position, hand dominance, remaining season and goals through shared decision making [r2].

grading.system: Clinical grading by laxity and endpoint, with the Stener lesion and avulsion fracture as modifiers

grades.description: Pain and tenderness over the ulnar MCP joint with no laxity on valgus stress (clinical convention).
Some laxity, but a firm endpoint on valgus stress [r3].
No firm endpoint with the thumb in 30° of MCP flexion and in extension [r3].
grades.prognosis: Operative treatment is recommended [r3]. Among 262 hand surgeons, 59% preferred surgery for a complete tear without a Stener lesion [r16].

grades.grade: Grade III with Stener lesion or displaced avulsion fracture
grades.description: Complete rupture with the aponeurosis interposed, or a displaced bone fragment [r1,r2].
grades.prognosis: Strong consensus for surgery: 95% for Stener lesions and 79% for displaced avulsion fractures [r16]

timeframes.summary: Ligament healing runs through inflammation, proliferation and remodelling over many months, but protection is needed for the first weeks. No controlled trial defined the duration of nonoperative immobilisation, so the phases are an illustrative clinical model. Reported postoperative times are athletes returning to sport within 5–8 weeks in a review [r8] and a mean return to duty of 11.8 weeks in soldiers [r11].

healing.description: Pain, swelling and bruising; protect the thumb and arrange diagnosis (clinical)
Thumb MCP immobilised after repair or for a partial tear. Immobilisation lasted 4–6 weeks in most series of chronic reconstruction [r7].
Graded range of motion then resisted pinch; protocols vary by repair quality and sport [r2]
Scar remodels; strength and tolerance of valgus loads continue to improve (clinical)

milestones.label: Diagnosis and surgical decision
milestones.note: Earlier intervention generally gives better results in a systematic review of surgical repair [r8]

milestones.label: End of immobilisation
milestones.note: Immobilisation typically lasted 4–6 weeks in chronic reconstruction series; nonoperative duration is a clinical convention [r7]

milestones.label: Athletes return to sport after surgery
milestones.note: Return was often within 5–8 weeks after surgery in a review, with rates up to 98.1% [r8]

milestones.label: Return to unrestricted duty
milestones.note: Mean 11.8 weeks, with 94.3% of 35 soldiers back within 3 months of surgery [r11]

timeframes.returnToSport: Return is criteria-based. A review reported athletes returning to sport within 5–8 weeks of surgery [r8], and soldiers returned to duty at a mean of 11.8 weeks [r11]. Return typically occurs with a protective thumb support, and the timing depends on repair quality and sport demands [r2].

symptoms: Pain at the ulnar side of the thumb MCP joint after a fall or valgus force
Swelling and bruising on the web side of the thumb
Weak or painful pinch and difficulty gripping or turning a key
A feeling of looseness or giving way of the thumb in pinch
A tender lump on the ulnar side of the MCP joint, in some complete tears
signs: Tenderness over the ulnar side of the MCP joint and the proximal phalanx base
Swelling and ecchymosis of the ulnar MCP region
Laxity with valgus stress, with a firm or absent endpoint [r3]
A palpable mass over the ulnar MCP joint, which suggests but does not confirm a Stener lesion [r4]
Weaker key pinch than the other side

subjective: Mechanism: ski pole fall, valgus force from a ball or opponent, rifle handling [r10,r11]
Time since injury, because chronic injuries are managed by reconstruction [r7]
Hand dominance, sport, season timing and work demands for surgical timing decisions [r2]
Pinch, grip and gripping a ski pole or racquet handle
Other injuries from the fall, for example scaphoid or wrist injury (clinical)
observation: Swelling and bruising over the ulnar MCP joint
Thumb posture at rest and during pinch
Any visible lump at the ulnar MCP joint
palpation: Ulnar MCP joint and proximal phalanx base tenderness
A mass proximal to the MCP joint on the ulnar side, as a possible Stener lesion [r4]
Radial MCP joint, thumb CMC joint, snuffbox and scaphoid for associated injury
rangeOfMotion: MCP flexion and extension compared with the other thumb
IP joint motion, which should be preserved
strength: Key pinch, tip pinch and three-jaw pinch compared with the other side
neuro: Digital sensation on both sides of the thumb
Radial sensory nerve territory if there is dorsoradial pain (clinical)
functional: Ability to pinch a key or turn a door handle
Sport-specific grip such as holding a pole, ball or racquet
Rifle or tool grip in military and manual work [r11]

specialTests.name: Valgus stress test at 0° and 30° of MCP flexion
specialTests.purpose: Grade collateral ligament laxity and distinguish a partial from a complete tear
specialTests.procedure: Stabilise the first metacarpal. Apply a gentle radially directed (valgus) force to the proximal phalanx with the MCP in extension and in about 30° of flexion, and compare with the other thumb.
specialTests.positive: No solid endpoint at 30° flexion and in extension indicates a complete tear. A firm endpoint indicates a partial tear [r3]. Pain may limit the test, so imaging helps. Sensitivity and specificity of stress testing were not found in the sources retrieved.

specialTests.name: Palpation for a Stener mass
specialTests.purpose: Screen for a displaced ligament stump
specialTests.procedure: Palpate the ulnar MCP region proximal to the joint for a tender lump while the thumb is relaxed.
specialTests.positive: A mass over the ulnar MCP joint is commonly palpated in a Stener lesion, but a granulation mass has mimicked it (a pseudo-Stener lesion) [r4]. Only 27% of 262 hand surgeons considered examination alone enough to detect a Stener lesion, versus 78% for diagnosing a complete tear [r16].

specialTests.name: Ultrasound for a Stener lesion (imaging test)
specialTests.purpose: Identify a displaced UCL stump superficial to the adductor aponeurosis
specialTests.procedure: High-resolution ultrasound over the ulnar MCP joint, by an experienced operator, including dynamic assessment.
specialTests.positive: Absent UCL fibres with a heterogeneous mass-like area proximal to the MCP joint [r13].
specialTests.sensitivity: 96% (95% CI 89–99) for Stener lesions, from 17 studies

clinicalRules.name: Decision between nonoperative and operative care
clinicalRules.description: Management depends on the grade of injury and on the presence of a Stener lesion or large avulsion fracture [r2]. Instability, rather than fragment size, was associated with surgery in avulsion fractures [r12]. If instability persists after a trial of nonoperative care, repair or reconstruction is considered [r1].

outcomeMeasures.name: QuickDASH
outcomeMeasures.use: Upper-limb disability; mean 4.2 after suture anchor repair in soldiers [r11]

outcomeMeasures.name: Key pinch and grip dynamometry
outcomeMeasures.use: Objective strength compared with the other hand; key pinch and grasp are the functions most affected [r1]

outcomeMeasures.name: Clinical valgus stress endpoint
outcomeMeasures.use: Firm endpoint at follow-up confirmed stability after repair [r11]

imaging.indication: Acute thumb injury, to look for an avulsion fracture and exclude other fractures
imaging.findings: Avulsion fragment from the proximal phalanx base [r12]. Stress radiographs are also used to separate partial from complete tears [r1].

imaging.indication: Suspected complete tear or Stener lesion; appropriate first-line imaging
imaging.findings: Pooled sensitivity and specificity were 95% and 94% in 9 ultrasound studies of Stener lesions, all at high risk of bias [r5]. A separate meta-analysis of 17 studies gave 96% and 90% for Stener lesions [r6].

imaging.indication: Ambiguous cases or other suspected injuries
imaging.findings: Pooled sensitivity 93% and specificity 98% for Stener lesions in 6 MRI studies [r5]. In a retrospective study of 96 surgical patients, MRI sensitivity was 97% and specificity 80% for UCL pathology but only 72–84% for subtypes, and it did not change the indication for surgery beyond a careful examination [r17].

differentials.name: Bennett fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Intra-articular fracture of the thumb metacarpal base after axial loading, with CMC joint pain and swelling at the base of the thumb, and radiographic fracture-subluxation.

differentials.name: Scaphoid fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Snuffbox tenderness and pain with axial thumb loading after a fall, rather than ulnar MCP laxity. Image if suspected.

differentials.name: Thumb MCP radial collateral ligament injury
differentials.distinguishing: Radial-sided MCP tenderness and laxity on varus stress; it was abnormal on ultrasound in 54.8% of one selected cohort and often coexists with the UCL injury [r14].

differentials.name: Thumb MCP dislocation or volar plate injury
differentials.distinguishing: Hyperextension injury with obvious deformity or volar swelling and tenderness, and loss of joint congruity on radiographs (clinical).

differentials.name: Paediatric physeal (Salter-Harris) fracture
differentials.distinguishing: In children, the thumb was one site with a higher proportion of Salter-Harris fractures in skiers and snowboarders, so a growth plate fracture should be excluded by radiograph [r18].

differentials.name: De Quervain's tenosynovitis
differentials.distinguishing: Gradual radial wrist pain over the first dorsal compartment without a valgus injury or ulnar MCP laxity.

differentials.name: Thumb CMC joint sprain or osteoarthritis
differentials.distinguishing: Pain and grind at the thumb base, with a stable MCP joint on valgus stress (clinical).

redFlags: A tender ulnar MCP mass with no firm endpoint on valgus stress: suspect a Stener lesion and arrange urgent hand surgical review, because a complete distal rupture commonly cannot heal without surgery [r4,r1].
A displaced avulsion fracture or MCP instability on radiographs: refer to hand surgery. 79% of 262 surgeons operate on displaced avulsion fractures [r16,r12].
A child or adolescent with thumb pain after a ski fall: image for a Salter-Harris fracture before assuming a ligament injury [r18].
Snuffbox tenderness or pain on axial thumb loading after the fall: image for scaphoid fracture and treat as a fracture until excluded (clinical).
Numbness at the thumb after surgery or injury: check for digital nerve injury. Transient sensory disturbance occurred in 3 of 35 soldiers after repair [r11].
Persistent instability, pain or weak pinch after a trial of immobilisation: refer for repair or reconstruction [r1,r7].

management.principles: Grade the injury with a valgus stress test and image when a complete tear or Stener lesion is possible. Partial tears with a firm endpoint are usually managed nonoperatively, and complete tears are managed surgically [r3]. Management depends on the grade and on any Stener lesion or large avulsion fracture, and the decision is shared [r2]. Among 262 hand surgeons, there was consensus for surgery for Stener lesions (95%) and displaced avulsion fractures (79%), while practice varied for complete tears without a Stener lesion (59% preferred surgery, 52% would also attempt nonoperative care, and 25% would never consider conservative care for any full-thickness tear) [r16]. A trial of nonsurgical care is followed by repair or reconstruction if instability persists [r1]. No randomised trials compare operative and nonoperative care, so most advice rests on cohorts, reviews and surveys [r8,r7].

medical.name: Surgical repair of a complete tear, including a Stener lesion
medical.description: Surgical management remains the standard for complete UCL tears, particularly with a Stener lesion, instability or failed conservative treatment, with favourable stability, strength and pain outcomes [r8]. Surgery is the consensus for Stener lesions (95% of 262 surgeons) [r16]. In 35 soldiers treated with suture anchor repair, all had a firm endpoint at follow-up and 94.3% returned to unrestricted duty within 3 months [r11]. No repair using native tissue equals the strength of the uninjured ligament [r1].

medical.name: Suture tape augmentation of repair
medical.description: Gave excellent short-term results and earlier return to function, with little long-term data [r1].

medical.name: Reconstruction for chronic injury
medical.description: A systematic review of 24 studies (331 patients, no randomised or comparative trials) found that direct repair was rarely feasible in chronic lesions, and anatomic tendon-graft reconstruction was the predominant and most consistently successful strategy. Immobilisation typically lasted 4–6 weeks. Risk of bias was fair to poor [r7].

medical.name: Nonoperative immobilisation (thumb spica) for a partial tear with a firm endpoint
medical.description: A firm endpoint on valgus stress indicates a partial tear for which nonoperative treatment is usually favoured [r3]. Partial or non-displaced tears can be managed nonoperatively [r4]. The duration of immobilisation was not defined in the sources retrieved.

medical.name: Nonoperative care for a complete tear without a Stener lesion
medical.description: Surgeons disagree: 59% preferred surgery, 52% would also attempt nonoperative treatment, and 25% would never consider conservative management [r16]. Shared decision making is central [r2].

medical.name: Cast treatment of a Stener lesion
medical.description: A complete distal rupture commonly cannot heal nonoperatively because the adductor aponeurosis is interposed [r4,r1]. 95% of surgeons favour surgery [r16].

medical.name: Avulsion fractures: surgery versus nonoperative care
medical.description: The debate is unresolved. In 114 patients, MCP joint instability rather than fragment size was the significant risk factor for surgery [r12]. Displaced fragments are an operative indication for 79% of surgeons [r16].

medical.name: Analgesia
medical.description: Simple analgesia for pain in the acute phase. No trial data were found for this injury.

physio.name: Early triage: stress test, referral and imaging requests
physio.description: Do a gentle valgus stress test at 0° and 30° [r3], request ultrasound for a possible Stener lesion [r5,r6], and refer early for a complete tear. Earlier intervention generally gave better results [r8].

physio.name: Thumb spica immobilisation, with the IP joint free
physio.description: Used for partial tears and after repair. Immobilisation typically lasted 4–6 weeks in series of chronic reconstruction [r7]. The nonoperative duration is a clinical convention.

physio.name: Postoperative rehabilitation with graded motion and strengthening
physio.description: Protocols vary with repair quality and sport demands [r2]. Athletes returned to sport within 5–8 weeks after surgery in a review [r8], and soldiers returned to duty at a mean of 11.8 weeks [r11]. There are no randomised comparisons of protocols.

physio.name: Protective thumb support and prevention advice for return to sport
physio.description: No injured skier in the Dolomites series used protective wrist or thumb supports. The authors suggested fall technique education, protective gloves and improved pole ergonomics. These were not tested [r10].

physio.name: Repeated forceful valgus stress testing of an acutely painful thumb
physio.description: Clinical teaching is that forceful repeated stress could displace a partial tear. This is not tested in the sources retrieved. Use a single gentle test and image instead (clinical).

education: The ligament on the inner side of the thumb joint is torn. If it is only partly torn it can heal in a splint, but a complete tear may need surgery.
A lump on the inner side of the thumb joint after the injury can mean the torn ligament has flipped out of place. This will not heal in a cast, so get it assessed quickly [r4].
Wear the support as advised and avoid pinching and sideways loads on the thumb until it is cleared.
After repair, most people and athletes return to their activities within a few weeks to 3 months [r8,r11].
Protective thumb support and careful pole technique are sensible when you return to skiing, although they have not been tested [r10].

rehab.overview: No trial has compared rehabilitation protocols for thumb UCL injury, and protocols vary with repair quality and sport demands [r2]. The stages below follow reported times (immobilisation of about 4–6 weeks [r7], return of athletes within 5–8 weeks after surgery [r8]) and common clinical convention. They apply to nonoperative care and to repairs, and the surgeon's protocol overrides them for K-wires, anchors or reconstruction. Progression depends on a firm valgus endpoint, pain and swelling, not on the calendar.

stages.name: Protect & settle
goals: Protect the healing UCL from valgus stress
Keep the IP joint, fingers and wrist moving
Teach one-handed function and wound or skin care
precautions: No valgus (radially directed) or pinch loading on the thumb MCP joint
Follow the surgeon's protocol for wires and splints
Monitor for infection and digital nerve symptoms after surgery [r11]

exercises.name: Thumb spica splint wear with the IP joint free
exercises.dosage: Worn full time except for supervised hygiene, for the period set by the surgeon (typically 4–6 weeks [r7])
exercises.cues: MCP supported, IP free to move

exercises.name: Active thumb IP flexion and extension
exercises.cues: Keep the MCP still in the splint

exercises.name: Active finger and wrist range of motion
exercises.cues: Keep the other fingers and wrist moving

exercises.name: Elevation and oedema control
exercises.dosage: Raise the hand above the elbow when resting (clinical)
exercises.cues: Gentle active fist and release if comfortable

exercises.name: Shoulder and elbow range of motion
exercises.cues: Stay active through the rest of the arm

progressionCriteria: Swelling and pain settled (pain 3/10 or less)
No signs of infection or nerve injury
Surgeon or physio confirms a firm endpoint where tested

stages.name: Protected motion
goals: Restore active MCP and thumb motion
precautions: Keep the splint on between exercise sessions and for risk activities
Avoid radial deviation stress of the thumb tip

exercises.name: Active thumb MCP flexion and extension
exercises.dosage: 10 repetitions, 4 times daily, within a pain-free arc

exercises.name: Thumb opposition to each fingertip (Kapandji progression)
exercises.cues: Reach to the index, middle, ring and little finger

exercises.name: Scar massage and desensitisation after surgery
exercises.dosage: 5 minutes, 3 times daily once the wound has healed
exercises.cues: Gentle circular pressure on the scar

exercises.name: Tendon glide for the thumb and fingers

progressionCriteria: Pain 2/10 or less with active motion
Active MCP flexion approaching the other side
Firm valgus endpoint on gentle clinical testing

stages.name: Strength & function
goals: Return to daily tasks without a splint
precautions: Avoid sudden valgus loads, for example contact or falls onto the hand
Use a thumb support for riskier tasks

exercises.name: Soft putty grip then pinch
exercises.dosage: 3 × 10 with 3–5 s holds, 3 times weekly; start with the softest putty
exercises.cues: Squeeze smoothly; keep the thumb aligned

exercises.name: Key, tip and three-jaw pinch strengthening
exercises.cues: Stop if the ulnar MCP aches

exercises.name: Wrist flexion and extension with light load
Farmer carry
exercises.cues: Neutral wrist and an even grip

progressionCriteria: Key pinch about 80% of the other side (a common clinical convention)
Pain 2/10 or less with loaded tasks
Firm valgus endpoint and no giving way

stages.name: Return to sport & work
goals: Return to sport, skiing and work
Protect the thumb in early return
precautions: Use a protective thumb support for the first return to contact sport or skiing (clinical convention)
Avoid falls onto the hand with a pole gripped; review technique

exercises.name: Sport-specific grip drills (ball, racquet, pole handle)
exercises.dosage: 3 sessions weekly, increasing duration and load
exercises.cues: Relaxed grip with an aligned thumb

exercises.name: Fall-technique practice
exercises.dosage: Practise in a controlled setting before returning to snow
exercises.cues: Let go of the pole and avoid landing on the outstretched thumb

exercises.name: Gradual return to contact or gripping sport
exercises.dosage: Start with non-contact drills, then partial and full training
exercises.cues: Support or tape the thumb for early sessions

progressionCriteria: Key pinch about 90% of the other side (a common clinical convention)
Confidence in gripping and falling safely

criteria: Firm endpoint on valgus stress, with no pain or giving way [r11]
Full pain-free thumb motion, with Kapandji opposition near the other side [r11]
Key pinch and grip about 90% of the other hand (a common clinical convention)
No residual swelling after sport-specific loading
Surgeon's clearance after repair or reconstruction [r2]
Protective thumb support for the first return to contact sport or skiing (clinical convention)

prognosis: Outcomes after surgical repair of complete tears were favourable for stability, range of motion, strength and pain in a review of 12 studies (335 patients), and athletes returned to sport at rates up to 98.1%, often within 5–8 weeks [r8]. In 35 soldiers treated with suture anchors, 94.3% returned to unrestricted duty within 3 months, with one superficial wound infection and three transient sensory disturbances [r11]. Various methods of surgical repair give excellent outcomes with a low incidence of complications [r1]. In chronic injuries, anatomic reconstruction restored stability and function with low re-rupture rates, but the studies were small and at fair to poor risk of bias [r7]. Untreated instability can reduce grip strength and lead to early MCP osteoarthritis [r4]. The nonoperative outcome of partial tears was not quantified in the sources retrieved.
prevention: Fall-technique education, protective gloves and improved pole ergonomics were suggested by the authors of a ski-injury series. None of the injured skiers used protective thumb supports. These measures are untested [r10].
Teach release of the pole handle during a fall rather than gripping it through the impact (clinical advice).
Use a protective thumb support or taping in the early return to contact sport (clinical).
Treat a painful, lax thumb MCP joint promptly so that a partial tear does not progress (clinical).
clinicalPearls: Test the thumb in both extension and about 30° of MCP flexion. No firm endpoint in either position suggests a complete tear [r3].
Never rely on palpation alone: a lump is common in a Stener lesion, but a granulation mass has mimicked one, and only 27% of surgeons felt examination alone could detect it [r4,r16].

Ultrasound is accurate for Stener lesions and is a reasonable first-line image. Reserve MRI for ambiguous cases [r5,r6]. MRI did not change the surgical indication beyond a careful examination in one cohort [r17].
A displaced distal rupture will not heal in a cast. Refer early rather than immobilising and waiting [r4,r1].
Terminology matters in notes and referrals: 'skier's' is acute and 'gamekeeper's' strictly means chronic attenuation [r3].
Check the radial collateral ligament and the extensor mechanism, because combined ultrasound abnormalities were frequent in a selected cohort [r14].

captions.text: A skier descends with a pole strapped to the right hand.
An edge catches and the skier is thrown sideways.
The hand lands on the snow with the pole handle gripped and the thumb held out.
The handle levers the thumb sideways, away from the hand, at the MCP joint.
Zooming into the base of the right thumb.

actions.text: UCL torn from its distal attachment
Stener lesion: stump displaced above the aponeurosis

captions.text: The ulnar collateral ligament runs from the metacarpal head to the base of the proximal phalanx.
A valgus force pulls the proximal phalanx away from the ulnar side and stretches the ligament.
The ligament fails, most often at its distal attachment on the proximal phalanx.
In a complete tear the stump can flip proximally, above the adductor aponeurosis.
This is a Stener lesion. The aponeurosis blocks the ends from meeting, so a cast will not heal it.
Healthy ligament: crimped type I collagen fibres aligned along the line of load.
Under valgus load the crimp straightens and the fibres stretch.
Beyond the elastic range, fibrils slide and begin to fail.
Sequential fibre failure ends in rupture at the attachment.
Torn capillaries bleed into the gap.
Neutrophils then macrophages clear debris over the first days.
Fibroblasts bridge the gap, but only if the torn ends are held together. A Stener lesion prevents this.
Collagen remodels along the line of load. A repaired ligament does not regain native strength.
